utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are allowing you to complete your examination-in-chief in relation to Bosnia. I expect your questions to be focused and specific and non-leading, and please don't ask questions, "Is it so-and-so or ..." where the latter question, the alternative, is clearly suggesting the answer to the witness. I'm told that tabs 28 -- yes. So that matter has already been dealt with. And we're expecting you to conclude in the first session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Professor Kostic occupied the highest posts in Yugoslavia. I don't know how I can go on with leading questions if he should answer simply what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Kostic, in the book "The Balkan Odyssey," Lord Owen, on page 182 of this book, which has been exhibited, writes about Mladic, but I would like to quote only one brief passage. "When in June 1991, when the Serb Croat war began, Ratko Mladic was Chief of Staff of the 9th Army Corps based Knin. Like other corps, this one was disintegrating because the personnel started declaring themselves as Croats or Slovenes, and leaving the JNA in order to join their national armies. Some of them left army service altogether or left the country completely. Those who remained serving on the JNA had no longer any freedom and many were besieged by the Croatian army in their barracks, which is one of the reasons why the JNA reacted so forcefully in places like Vukovar. At that stage, a traditional civil war developed --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The accused is again on the Croatia indictment, and he was actually told he can only deal with Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Milosevic. Move on to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this question where Lord Owen, who represented the European Community in the entire peace process and chaired the peace conference speaks about a traditional civil war, my question to Mr. Kostic would relate to both Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a civil war there, or was it, on the contrary, an aggression, an occupation, or something like that? To the best of your knowledge from that time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that both in Croatia and, unfortunately, later in Bosnia we had a typical textbook civil war, with a proviso that it was waged between two ethnicities, between Serbs and Croats in Croatia, whereas in Bosnia it took an even more drastic form; everybody waged war against everybody. For a while, there was a war between the coalition of Muslims and Croats against Serbs. Later, Croats and Muslims fought one another, and that is the most traditional example, the most classic example of a civil war. And if you allow me, I have a CD here, and four minutes of it will tell you more than a half hour of my talking, because that's something I said on Sarajevo TV that caused an outcry in the Croatian democracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. You have answered the question, and I do not wish to listen to the CD. Ask another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, what kind of efforts were taken by the SFRY Presidency to stop the conflict from spreading on to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions, already in the second half of 1991, we evaluated the political and security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and issued very serious warnings that the situation was getting more tense with every day. And we warned also that unless all the three ethnic leadership in Bosnia steered to another course, there will be a civil war in that country with no winners. In addition to that, in its reduced composition, the SFRY Presidency organised a Conference on Yugoslavia on the 3rd of January, involving various movements, individuals from all over Yugoslavia, but mostly from Bosnia. Unfortunately, members of the SDA, the Socialist Democratic Action Party of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, were not taking part, and the same goes for the Croatian Democratic Union of Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have this footage that Mr. Kostic has offered? If it is ready in the AV booth, we can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's only three and a half minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What does it show? What does it show, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an interview I gave to a Sarajevo television studio called Club 92 -- or 91, on the eve of the Catholic Christmas, after all discussions that took place in the Presidency and just before the war in Bosnia started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it add anything to the comments that you have just made about the nature of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It adds something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we'll not hear it. Proceed to another matter, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know and what can you tell us about the so-called Belgrade Initiative? Let me draw your attention to tab 72, where we have your book, and the text of the Belgrade Initiative is included. You can open this tab and use it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Belgrade Initiative was signed in August 1991. The highest ranking representatives of Serbia took part in the formulation of this initiative, including you and Mr. Momir Bulatovic from the Presidency of Montenegro. There was Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but not as a representative of the Serb people but as speaker of the Bosnian Assembly. There were other participants in this Belgrade Initiative, and you can see that from the document under the tab. The principal purpose of the Belgrade Initiative was to define a framework for a way to organise all those who wish to continue living in a common state. Thus, the Belgrade Initiative opened a door to all those who believed it was in their interest to continue living in one common state. They had the option of committing themselves along those principles, because elections in Macedonia, for instance, and -- were not conducted yet -- or, rather, the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there some sort of draft proposal for the way to organise a future state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A proposal was made, and the main thing about it was that this future state should have a two-Chamber parliament, one of which should be representing republics with proportional representations, thus ensuring equal rights to all republics and all entities in that future state without the possibility of anybody being out-voted by anybody else. That's in tab 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard many speeches here, including Mesic's speech and testimony given here to the effect that we had pushed the so-called close-knit firm federation. Now, look at this document in 84 and see what we actually proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Belgrade Initiative, which we haven't found in the book, is actually Exhibit 338, tab 9, or D272.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. Robinson. I didn't even tender it because it's already exhibited. I just wanted the witness to comment upon it, because he was one of the key politicians in Yugoslavia of that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, don't miss the point. You should be providing this information. It should not be left to Judge Kwon. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does paragraph 1 say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yugoslavia is a common state of equal peoples, republics, and citizens. "2 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read all the paragraphs. Look at the most important ones, such as 4.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republics in Yugoslavia shall enact their constitutions independently, whereas the bodies of Yugoslavia shall act within their purview independently, as established by the Constitution of Yugoslavia. "Republics in Yugoslavia shall independently establish international relations and conclude international covenants outside areas governed by the Constitution of Yugoslavia. Such relationships and covenants may not be to the detriment of the common interests within Yugoslavia or to the detriment of the interests of other peoples and republics in Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 5.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republics and nations in Yugoslavia may step out of Yugoslavia in the way and according to the procedure stipulated by the Constitution and the legislation of Yugoslavia, with the proviso that interests of other nations and republics may not be damaged."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 7.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yugoslavia shall be based on the principle of equality of Yugoslav peoples and republics. National minorities shall have all minority and human rights recognised for them as established by the corresponding international covenants."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 9.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9: "Market economy, equality of all forms of property, freedom of movement of people, commodities, capital," et cetera, "and freedom of entrepreneurship, are the basic principles on which economic life in Yugoslavia shall develop."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 10.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10: "In Yugoslavia, state authorities shall be organised on the principle of division of power in the form of multi-party parliamentary republics based on the rule of law and social justice."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These proposals for organising internal relationships within Yugoslavia, what kind of powers are envisaged for the bodies of Yugoslavia? That is written in item III. What was planned? What were to be the common elements exercised at the level of the joint state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was envisaged that at the level of Yugoslavia, legislation in the area of banking, monetary policy, customs policy, foreign economic relations should be adopted, as well as laws governing the tax system, trading within the Yugoslav market, science and technology, defence of Yugoslavia, the position, the composition and the use of the Yugoslav army, representation of Yugoslavia abroad and foreign relations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about 5, freedoms and rights of citizens?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Freedoms and rights of citizens envisaged by international laws and covenants. I said already that the parliament was supposed to have two Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So an Assembly, the president of the republic, the government. Those were the bodies envisaged by this proposal. Can you tell us very briefly, who was Adil Zulfikarpasic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Adil Zulfikarpasic was one of the most prominent and very respected intellectuals from Sarajevo who first joined the SDA party of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic but soon made a turnabout, distanced himself from the SDA and formed another party with Mr. Muhamed Filipovic, a Bosniak party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did he make this turnaround from the SDA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at the first rallies of the SDA that he attended on the eve of the first multi-party elections to the parliament, he had the impression that that party was becoming more extremist, more fundamentalist every day in its policies, and he even says in one of his writings that some of his friends, officials from Germany, from their liberal parties abroad, that he had invited -- he meant to invite to come to Bosnia and Herzegovina but gave up when he saw how extremist these rallies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He writes that he cancelled all these visits of his foreign friends when he saw the iconography of the party, the SDA party. He speaks about it at length in one of his interviews that we will not deal with separately here. But do you have that interview he gave to the Nin magazine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me see if I can find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can't, I'll ask the following: Are you aware that as he was one of Izetbegovic's sponsors and closest associates for a long time, he came to see me in connection with the Belgrade Initiative?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that we had a lengthy conversation about all these topics at the time. And could you please put on the ELMO just a brief quotation of his where we can see what he discussed with me, inter alia. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which tab number is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the tab number, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zulfikarpasic's interview was too long, which is why I did not include it in the tabs. So I will present just a brief quotation from it. It's from the weekly Nin, and the interview is 50 pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just the part that's been highlighted. Could you please some in on it. And I will ask you to read what he says here about what I suggested to him, the part that's been circled.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He proposed that the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia be chosen in alphabetical order and that Bosnia and Herzegovina provide the first president. Milosevic told me that he agrees that a Muslim be the president of the country for five years, with competencies similar to those enjoyed by the president of France; that is, that he be able to appoint military leaders, diplomats, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was a time where we were trying to find a way to set up Yugoslavia again and have relations as friendly as possible with, first of all, the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you imagine a Greater Serbia of which Alija Izetbegovic would be president for five years with all these powers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very important detail, which only goes to confirm what I said at the outset, that there was no intention whatsoever of establishing a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the Belgrade Initiative, this new Yugoslav union, would it have been open to Croatia and Slovenia, those who had left and who might possibly want to join again?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was envisaged as open to all, even if they did not join right away. But later on, if they concluded that such a union would suit them, they would still be able to join it. These talks between Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic and you on the basis of the Belgrade Initiative are well known publicly, and they are referred to as the historical agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who accepted the Belgrade Initiative and who rejected it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what Mr. Zulfikarpasic himself writes, he didn't come to talk to you in Belgrade on his own initiative. He was authorised by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to discuss this agreement between Serbs and Muslims. Alija had told him that the Serbs saw him, Alija, in a bad light and that it might be better if it was Mr. Zulfikarpasic who attended the talks. Mr. Zulfikarpasic agreed to this, and he accepted the agreement drawn up in Belgrade. He went back to Sarajevo and informed Mr. Alija Izetbegovic of this. It seems that on that very day or the next day Alija Izetbegovic was to travel to America. He agreed with the agreement but said that it should wait until he got back from the USA. When he did get back from the USA, he said that the agreement reached by Mr. Zulfikarpasic in Belgrade was no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw the document in tab 84. What about the commission of the Presidency which prepared this Belgrade agreement? And you were its vice-president. It's a document of the 5th of September, 1991, and it's in tab 32.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already commented on this document. The Belgrade Initiative and that document of the 5th of September, which is in fact only a communique whereby Mr. Stjepan Mesic spoke at the inaugural meeting in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a document that the entire Presidency headed by Mesic accepted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but now we're looking at it from another angle. What you said in connection with Mesic is one thing. Now we are discussing the Belgrade Initiative and this document in view of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Zulfikarpasic, at the time, was -- he was not mentioned in your response to my previous question, but now we are discussing Bosnia. I won't dwell on this because I want to get through the questions as quickly as possible. I won't dwell on his standpoints, the description of the political situation. Zulfikarpasic, as you said, speaks of the extremist and fundamentalist nature taken on more and more by the Party of Democratic Action. Before and after all the events mentioned by Zulfikarpasic - and he mentions all those rallies and so on - were there any clear indications of Izetbegovic's fundamentalist standpoints and those of the ruling Muslim leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was very evident. First of all, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic is the author of the so-called Islamic Declaration, which, although it was drawn up as a platform, represents very extremist standpoints and extremist views on the organisation of a Muslim state. In one place in that declaration, Mr. Izetbegovic expressly states that in such an Islamic state there is no place for any other political or religious option. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic stated in public that everything that happened in Bosnia during the civil war had taken place 20 or 30 years too early, because 20 or 30 years later on, in a peaceful manner, Bosnia would have become a Muslim majority state, and the Muslims could have organised an Islamic state because they were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any indications that in that independent Bosnia the Serbs would not be equal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many indications of this in everyday life. But the grossest indicator was that attempts were made to reach decisions on the most fateful issues in Bosnia by out-voting. The leadership of the Muslims and Croats, against the will of the Serbs and without their presence in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, made decisions on all important questions that touched on the position of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina - not just of Yugoslavia - literally stated that Bosnia was made up of three constituent peoples; Muslims, Serbs and Croats, and no people could, to the detriment of the two others -- no two peoples to the detriment of the third could issue a decision, least of all on a major issue pertaining to the fate of the peoples. So that in early 1992, the Bosnian Presidency operated without its two representatives of the Serbian people. And it was a collective organ, a collective head of state, just as the Yugoslav Presidency was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly that issued the decision on a referendum after 2.00 a.m., when the Serbs had gone for a break, was it made with or without the Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw a brief clip where Lord Carrington says this was illegal. Did the Presidency of the SFRY draw attention in a timely manner to the unlawfulness of such an action?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the standpoint of the Presidency about this and the standpoint of other organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the SFRY and all the other political and state organs pointed out that any attempt to make decisions or adopt solutions to which all three nations in Bosnia had not agreed would lead to civil war. Unfortunately, this proved to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the Presidency at the time, did you feel it was justified, this fear of the Serbs in Bosnia, that in a unitary and independent Bosnia they would fall under the domination of a political group which one of its founders, Adil Zulfikarpasic, described as extremist and fundamentalist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We felt that the Serbs had good reason to fear this, but it was the Serbs in Bosnia who felt it most. The Serbs in Bosnia had many negative experiences from World War II, and it was difficult for them to believe at the outset that the Muslims and the Croats would reach decisions on such important issues without the Serbs, and therefore they were afraid that they would be constantly out-voted and that all issues, including issues pertaining to their status, would be made in the same way. They were afraid of having the status of a minority in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at a brief clip showing the Reis-Ul-Ulema, Mustafa Ceric, which shows what his standpoint was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the word that's missing from the transcript before "Mustafa Ceric"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Reis-Ul-Ulema, the chief Muslim religious leader in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] It's God's order to us and human obligation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So jihad is God's order and a human obligation. Let's look at another brief clip where Izetbegovic is shown and the Mujahedin formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is sufficient. What could the Serbs in Bosnia think in this kind of atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, have you a date for this and any indication of what it is? It was absolutely meaningless to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a review of the Mujahedin Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness if he can indicate what it is and when it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see any pictures on the monitor. I could only hear the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, so much for that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, what do you know about the peace efforts on the part of the international community and cooperation between the representatives of the three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which resulted in the Cutileiro Plan? What do you know about that, and what do you know about the Cutileiro Plan as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about those steps towards peace, I do know something because I was the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency still at the time, and what I know is this: The international community had launched an initiative with the intention of preventing the escalation of a civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the Presidency of Yugoslavia, in its reduced form, albeit, and also the authorities, the state authorities and the political authorities in Serbian and Montenegro, gave their support to the efforts made by the international community unreserved. The Cutileiro Plan provided for a sort of principle of cantonal set-up for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be useful, because we have tab 62, you have a map from the Cutileiro Plan. Perhaps it would be a good idea to place it on the overhead projector and then you can indicate to us what the idea was for this cantonal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina for those following these proceedings to be able to have a better idea of this. Here we can see the map, but it's all written -- the legend is in Cyrillic, but the horizontal lines is the Serb area, the white is the Muslim area, the dark area is the Croat area, and the diagonal lines are Sarajevo. So it's only Sarajevo that has these diagonal lines which has special treatment. It is a separate canton. The white area is the Muslim area, the horizontal lines are the Serb area, and the dark areas are the Croatian areas.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Cutileiro Plan, an attempt was made to come by a solution which would in fact mean an end to the civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or Cutileiro's plan came before the civil war broke out.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the civil war. That's right. But the basic idea underlying it was that an organisation should be made for Bosnia-Herzegovina as being a whole, one entity, but on the cantonal principle, in such a way that each community or ethnic community would have its own canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's own canton, and an explanation is given there in the legend. Now, tell us, please, when the negotiations were completed, did all three sides accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All three sides adopted the Cutileiro Plan, including Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. However, as soon as Bosnia-Herzegovina was -- had become a member of the United Nations, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his signature from the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't withdraw the signature then, he withdrew his signature before Bosnia and Herzegovina became a member of the UN, but never mind. Do you know anything about this retraction of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I ask the witness, do you know anything about this plan, because that's twice you have had to be corrected by the accused, who is effectively giving evidence here. Did this plan come into existence while you were in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did, except that we as the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, can I ask you, what was your direct involvement with it as a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Bonomy, I didn't come into direct -- or didn't have any direct involvement with the plan. I didn't work on the plan because the Yugoslav state Presidency was not involved, included in the definition of the Cutileiro Plan. All I know is that as the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency from those days, that time, when there was mention of the Cutileiro Plan, we were all vitally interested in finding a peaceful settlement to the crisis in Bosnia. And from that point of view I can certainly talk about those times. I do know, for example, that the US ambassador, Mr. Zimmerman, in fact prevailed upon Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and persuaded him not to accept the Cutileiro Plan, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that this witness is very distant from this plan and that it's one that ought to be dealt with through a witness with more direct knowledge, but that's, I dare say, a question of the weight that the Tribunal -- or the Trial Chamber can give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, in the drafting of the Cutileiro Plan, we had the participation of the three sides in Bosnia. No one outside Bosnia-Herzegovina and Cutileiro and his associates took part in it. They agreed amongst themselves, and the map was published once the plan had been adopted. And we all applauded the agreement because we thought that they had resolved the problem in Bosnia, and that's a fact. We don't have to go into the details of how it came about. The negotiations took place in Lisbon, where the three negotiating parties from Bosnia-Herzegovina were present, whereas this map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All you've just -- it's not for you to give evidence, as you've apparently chosen not to, and all of this is material that plainly there's little point in presenting through this witness. It seems to me that it's a complete waste of the limited time you have to deal with matters that this witness has personal knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. It will be a question of the weight that we can attach to this witness's evidence on the Cutileiro Plan in view of the level of his involvement in it. Let us proceed quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were shown a map a moment ago of the cantonal division. It was published by the mass media. A territorial distribution of the canton of this kind, or the map, can it represent a groundwork for the territorial expansion of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In no case can it do that. As you can see, the cantons were devised in such a way that the large part, that is to say the horizontal lines that -- the area lined that way that should have come to the Serbs in Western Bosnia, was completely cut off, as we can see, according to the cantonal plan; cut off with the cantons and territories under Croat or Muslim control, envisaged for the Croats and the Muslims. And as you can see, this white area here, that was supposed to represent once again a Muslim canton, so that even if you just glance at this map of Bosnia and the proposed cantons, which were agreed upon and accepted and adopted by the Yugoslav side as well with great enthusiasm, indicates that we could not speak about territorial pretensions of any kind on the part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Cutileiro Plan envisage Bosnia as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs accepted that, did they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The Serbs accepted being an independent state but with this cantonal set-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go on to another subject. How did the JNA come to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole scenario as to the position of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina followed a similar pattern as it did in Slovenia and especially it resembled the way this was done in Croatia. As we in Bosnia-Herzegovina also had a large portion of the military industry there and many barracks during peacetime that were deployed and dispersed across Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had a lot of interest in achieving an agreement with respect to the relationship they would have and the attitude to the Yugoslav army and the soldiers in the barracks, because we were very afraid that the scenario of Croatia was not repeated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor Kostic. Now, you in your capacity as vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency and the presiding officer in the reduced Presidency on the 26th of April, 1992, had a meeting with Alija Izetbegovic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where the meeting was held, who attended it, and then we'll go on to discuss it after that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in Skopje on the 26th of April, 1992, on behalf of the staff of the Supreme Command. Together with me, General Blagoje Adzic travelled to Skopje, and the host in Skopje was Mr. Kiro Gligorov. Up until that -- or, rather, the meeting came about after several attempts on my part, unsuccessful, to establish communication with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and at that meeting in Skopje we discussed how, in what way we could solve the question of the position of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on that occasion Mr. Alija Izetbegovic told us that the Yugoslav People's Army could stay on for five years in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He did ask that the commanders of that army, of those units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, be Muslims, that is to say to have Muslim officers from the composition of the Yugoslav people's army, and Mr. Blagoje Adzic said as a joke, "Then you can propose me as the commander of the Green Berets, for example." Well, that was a sort of joke, but we did note that the question of the JNA's position in Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be solved successfully until a political solution had been found and until a supreme civilian command had been established over the army, which implied and meant the return of the representatives of the Serbs to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's take a look at tab 5, where we see -- it says here some sound records. So this is something that has been taken from a tape recording, not very successfully, I have to say, and it is found in tab 5. They are records or phonetic notes between Branko Kostic and Blagoje Adzic with the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, in Skopje on the 26th of April, 1992. And the discussions began at 1300 hours. You mentioned Gligorov a moment ago, who was your host. Now, Gligorov was the president of Macedonia, was he not? Before that, that is to say before the 26th of April, 1992, did Macedonia decide to step down from Yugoslavia and to have the army withdraw from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the army indeed withdraw from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the army did withdraw from Macedonia without a single bullet having been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any outstanding issues to be settled between Belgrade and Skopje with respect to the withdrawal of the army from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no contentious issues, and I kept stressing that that two-way communication with Mr. Gligorov was highly successful, very constructive, and this meeting that we organised - that is to say Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and I with Mr. Gligorov - was the result of that expression of goodwill and the good communication with we had with Mr. Gligorov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what was the date of the withdrawal of the army from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be honest, I can't give you an exact date now. I can't say. But I can check it out in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly when? Roughly when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't tell you exactly. Well, by the break I'll be able to find that and give you an answer, to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us briefly go through the transcript of an audio recording of the talks. On page 1, in the last paragraph, you emphasise the following: You say, "I think it is a favourable circumstance that we are meeting in Skopje, Macedonia, which until yesterday was part of Yugoslavia and with which we settled all those issues, including the status of the JNA, in a very fair manner without any conflict or bloodshed in a manner that made it possible for us to talk."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that took place before your talks, before these 26th of April talks. And you also say that you expressed the need to have the meeting in view of the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised as an independent state by a certain number of countries, and in view of the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army was present there and that most of the military industry we built together was located there, and so on and so forth, and that the question of a political status of the three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina had not yet been regulated and that to all intents and purposes there was a civil war going on there, and that talks should start and each for their own part should do as much as they can to put a stop to that war there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- while constituting Bosnia and Herzegovina as independent and autonomous state. So is that the substance of what you on behalf of the Presidency proposed to Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now here when it comes to Mr. Izetbegovic, what does he say? Let's take a look at that. He says that nothing can be finally decided because he doesn't have the competence and authority to do so, but that we could begin the talks.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that talks can be held but that he couldn't take any responsibility upon himself for doing anything. And he goes on to say in the third paragraph: "A new situation has arisen, not only as a result of the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina but also of Yugoslavia, a proclamation of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's on page 2, but it's Izetbegovic speaking. So those are two facts. Those are two facts that call for the issue of the JNA or, rather, its elements, and he's talking -- referring to elements stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is there any contention to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing contentious there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Which are in Bosnia-Herzegovina must be solved so that there should not be violence or illegal measures taken. It would be a good idea if they were dealt with through negotiation." That's what he says. He speaks about the need to avoid all sorts of violence, because until then, as far as the army is concerned, they had no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic even told us at lunch, in the presence of Mr. Gligorov, that in all the places where JNA units were stationed, the situation was calmed and there were no inter-ethnic or inter-religious conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, he goes on to say that stage by stage they should leave Bosnia, mainly personnel who are not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 3: "Gradually, of course, possibly step-by-step so that the personnel who are not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina should leave." I'll skip a bit and then come back to it. Is that what actually happened under that order of the Presidency, all JNA members who were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro withdrew from the territory of BH?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's very soon after this meeting. This meeting was on the 26th of April, and your decision was on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on the 19th of May that year, Serbia and Montenegro did not have a single soldier stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he says, number one, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, among the military personnel, should stay. Number two, the armed forces must accept the authority of the civil government of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, they must recognise the Supreme Command, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina or another body, depending on what it will be based on under a future agreement. And then in another passage toward the bottom of that page, he says the ethnic composition of the JNA is currently disrupted, of the part of the JNA stationed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is severely disrupted. "I do not blame the army for that," he says. "A lot of things played a part. We also played a part by denying the deployment of our recruits." That's what Izetbegovic himself is saying. He's saying in no uncertain terms, "We denied new arrivals from Bosnia into the JNA."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me that since quite some time now Mr. Milosevic is giving evidence. He is quoting things from a huge document. He's making comments about what it means, what is quoted there. I don't think that this is the proper way to proceed. This is an extensive document, and we hear from Mr. Milosevic all sorts of little snips of it, and I am not in a position to follow what's really meant at a certain stage, and the witness actually isn't asked anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is an extensive document. You must put your questions precisely. Focus the witness. Don't read long passages, and refrain from comments while you're reading, because you're not giving evidence. What is the precise question that you have for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. Are you saying that I am not allowed to quote from this document, that the witness should quote from it instead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can quote for it, but don't make comments while you're quoting. That is what the Prosecutor is complaining of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- can I ask the witness, have you read this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have I read it? Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document reflecting the talks that I had with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to be clear about. So it seems a pointless exercise, going through it line by line, when we can read it for ourselves. I'm just wondering why Mr. Milosevic doesn't ask you questions about what you ultimately agreed or disagreed upon with Mr. Izetbegovic, and then we could move on. We can read it for ourselves after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it seems to us that this is a document that we could admit in its entirety. The witness participated in it. Do you have specific questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is one of the key issues, why the ethnic composition of the army was unbalanced; what Izetbegovic himself gave as a reason for this unbalance in the ethnic composition of military personnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is common knowledge, and I've said this before, certain national leaderships one by one started refusing to send their recruits to the army any more. First the Slovenes, then Croats, and as I said, Muslims a bit later. In my view, it is particularly pertinent that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic himself notes this disbalance in the ethnic composition of the army and army units stationed in Bosnia, and he says himself that it's a result of the fact that the Muslim leadership had stopped sending their conscripts to the army. It also has to do with the fact that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic later formed his own Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what we saw on that footage?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that on that video. You can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he say unequivocally they stopped their conscripts from joining the army any more?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he say, in fact, that he doesn't blame the army for that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he say that it is a real task to re-establish peace and have people return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you quote from the second passage on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is actually a fruitless exercise to put to the witness, "Does he say that?" and the witness simply says "Yes." I mean, either it should be just moved on or the witness would have to tell what he remembers from this in addition to what we see here in the transcript. I can't really see what use it is to put -- to go on like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution not follow this practice when you introduced something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you did. You did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But that's -- I mean, what should be done and I think what the Prosecution did when you have a document, we quote from the document, giving the passage what we are quoting, and then ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it is tantamount to the same thing. It's a practice that has been used by both parties. It's not one that I'm accustomed to, certainly coming from the -- from my jurisdiction, but we have endorsed its use here. Mr. Milosevic could, nonetheless, I believe, try to identify issues that arise from -- from this interview and put them to the -- to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor Kostic, look at the second paragraph on page 5. What does it say? "To return to their homes --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbs to Serb homes, Muslims to Muslim homes, Croats to Croat homes. People should return home and have their security guaranteed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you indicate the English page number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's in -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is the second paragraph from the bottom, towards the bottom of the paragraph, the sentence starting with: "First of all, it should be made possible for them ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 5 in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, we found it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third paragraph from the bottom on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What people are being referred to here? What people who had been driven out of their homes are being referred to by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic speaks about all the three constituent peoples of Bosnia; Serbs, Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he talking about them because they are constituent peoples, all of them, or because what they have in common is that they had been driven out from some places?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those places were the battlefield of very important conflicts, and of course there were many people displaced from all the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the middle of page 6, this very large paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one that starts with, "The idea is acceptable ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me find it. Yes. It's on page 5, the last large paragraph before "Branko Kostic." That's in English. And could you please read what he says. He accepts to create conditions for hundreds if thousands of people. Will you go on reading this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For hundreds of thousands of people who have left their homes on all sides, because in Bosnia and Herzegovina most of the victims are Serbs and Muslims, and Croats to a lesser extent. So there are a lot of Serbian refugees and a lot of Muslim refugees who have left their homes. First of all, it should be made possible for them to return to their homes, and they should be guaranteed safety. This can only be done by a new force that would not be purely Serb or purely Muslim, but a new force, actually a joint Bosnian and Herzegovinian force that would be so organised from top down; the soldiers, the command officers, the military, the tasks it would set itself as a goal."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's the end of his contribution here. Now, you ask him a question before General Adzic starts speaking. Since he himself said that the -- that force should not be purely Serb or Muslim but must be joint, you ask him: "How do you imagine Joint Command over that army, because you have no Serb representatives in your Presidency?" What did he answer to that? What did Alija Izetbegovic say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says: "No Presidency in Bosnia and Herzegovina could possibly be equal without representatives of the Serb people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did they have any Serb representatives then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they hold a referendum without any Serbs in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They also made their application for recognition to the European Union without any Serb representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when he says, "Representation of all the constituent peoples --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says, "All we are saying, we are saying --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would appreciate the reference really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is this from? The interpreters are trying to find it. Page 6?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What he just quoted,

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: "No Presidency in Bosnia and Herzegovina without a Serb in it will be able to guarantee equality, without representatives of the Serbian people." That's what he quoted. And then further down in the same passage, although it's a bit disjointed in translation, it's not so compact as it sounds in the original --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says: "The Presidency is currently deficient because these two are absent," meaning that there are no Serb representatives in the Presidency. "How can we solve that? Can we organise some new additional elections or maybe get those two to return or maybe achieve some sort of agreement in later negotiations? Because a new type of supreme organ is envisaged, a new forum or a new organ, but in each of these bodies there would be equal representation of all."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the next page, you see you ask him how he sees the future of the peace conference.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says: "The last time, I told Cutileiro, Please bring all the parties together. Put forward a solution. We will accept it whatever it is."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come Cutileiro first made a plan, Izetbegovic first signed it, then went back on his signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that our people say that nothing bad should be said about the dead, but the truth is that Mr. Izetbegovic was a very unreliable partner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He himself characterises the absence of Serbs on the Presidency as a deficiency, a shortcoming.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please be kind, because I don't want to spend too much time on this. Just tell us as briefly as you can. On page 12, Blagoje Adzic speaks. The first long passage.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The territory of BH ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, "On the territory of BH there are now fewer than 5 per cent members of the military."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that Blagoje Adzic speaking?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "This means that the JNA is fully manned mainly on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and over 80 per cent of the members of the JNA hail from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from that territory, and as many as 90 per cent are Serbs. That's not our fault, Mr. Izetbegovic, it's a mistake made by you and your leadership, because you told conscripts not to respond to mobilisation calls from the JNA, and you called on active duty officers to cross over to your side, to the Territorial Defence, which they are doing now on a relatively massive scale."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 9, Your Honour. Page 9 in the English, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does he go on to say? He says further: "Apart from that that -- despite that --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Despite that, thanks to its role, its purpose and mission, the JNA carried out its tasks mainly preventing major ethnic clashes. In areas where there were no JNA units and where various paramilitary formations were involved, disastrous clashes took place. For example, in Bosanski Brod, Kupres, Foca, Bijeljina, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where the JNA did not get involved, what does he say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There were major clashes, although propaganda says otherwise. For example, in Zvornik -- that life, for example, in Zvornik has been brought back to normal very quickly."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Izetbegovic says that no one should drive anyone out, referring to the departure of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And what is being discussed on pages 17 and 18? Who says this: "Mr. President, the siege of all barracks and military facilities must be lifted"? That's Blagoje Adzic speaking, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Izetbegovic asks, "Are there any barracks under siege?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Alija Izetbegovic doesn't know if there is a barracks under siege?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adzic replies, "Of course there are; Derventa, Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All this is under siege, Travnik, Zenica? All this is under siege? Today an order arrived from Efendic or a man called Siber, but Izetbegovic tries to justify himself by saying, "I read about this in the newspapers." Adzic said, "A person who wants peace shouldn't issue such orders. We can agree. We can discuss. We can coordinate matters, but to make such a decision unilaterally and issue the directive you know about, attacking barracks and so on, this means war."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a month before these talks we had in Skopje, a directive had been issued by the Muslim paramilitary formations to lay siege to all JNA barracks on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what's being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Adzic said: "If such an order was not issued with your approval, the person who issued it should be dismissed, because it leads to war." Izetbegovic, "Well, it was withdrawn the same moment but they were not dismissed." Well, was that order withdrawn? Were the barracks under siege? Was he telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was withdrawn or not. It may have been, but the barracks in Bosnia-Herzegovina remained under siege. In Sarajevo, in the Marshal Tito barracks, 300 young men of 16 or 17 remained under siege. They were cadets of a military school and they lived worse than in a concentration camp. We had no possibility of lifting the blockade of that barracks by the Muslim paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look - and we'll dwell on this only very briefly, we won't go into the entire text - but at the end you refer to various matters that you may explain, if you wish, but please look at page 36, which is at the very end, the last passage before Alija Izetbegovic speaks. "If pressure is exerted on us with respect to the status of the JNA --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "If there is a wish to exert pressure on us with respect to the status and place of the JNA and animate the international public, you can rest assured of one thing: We on our part will honour our two commitments. In other words, all your citizens, your nationals, we will send them from Serbia and Montenegro back to Bosnia and Herzegovina in a matter of several days, if necessary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the question on that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished quoting yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can he just finish reading the passage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Just as we will bring back people who are not from that area, who are not your nationals but ours. All the others stay there. You will then have to face the fact that you have Serbian people there armed and with their own army. You have Muslims and Croats armed and with their own army. You face a threat of a terrible civil war and bloodshed in which all will be killed, a total chaos, an all-out civil war there. "I think this is not a solution. We should talk about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please say whether the Presidency of the SFRY actually acted on this and returned all the citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the SFRY in its reduced composition, on the 4th of May, 1992, issued a decision that all members of the JNA should withdraw from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The constitution of the 27th of April of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had already been adopted. All those who were nationals of Serbia and Montenegro were to withdraw, and we acted on that. All of them were withdrawn. On the 19th of May, there were no longer any of our soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, we didn't have time to go through this rather extensive record in detail. At that meeting, did Alija Izetbegovic make any comments to you about the behaviour of the army or anything that might be seen as reprehensible conduct by the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for a moment. There was nothing like that. As soon as I returned from Skopje, because there was quite a lot of public interest in those talks of ours, which had been postponed many times, I made a public statement in which I said that I was very satisfied with the talks we had had with Mr. Izetbegovic in Skopje and that he had even stated that the army could stay there for five years, if necessary. Unfortunately, a few days later Mr. Izetbegovic held an extraordinary session of his reduced - not to say "Rump" - Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and demanded categorically that the Yugoslav army immediately withdraw from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And may I take this opportunity, because I owe Mr. Bonomy an answer to his question as to when the JNA was withdrawn from Macedonia, in view of the fact that this was settled in agreement with the Macedonian leadership, the withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia was done gradually and successively, in no great haste, but in March and April the JNA had been already withdrawn from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 4th of May, the Presidency issued a decision on withdrawal from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, without its Serbian representatives, issued a decision. What was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This session was practically held on the same day, and they declared the JNA to be an occupying army. They addressed the international public, even asking for foreign assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eight days previously, he had had no objections to the conduct of the JNA, but on the 4th of May when you issued the decision on withdrawing the army from Bosnia based on the results of your talks with him, he called them aggressors.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the foot of page 21 in the English, going on to page 22, which is a statement made by Izetbegovic, where he appears to suggest that paramilitary units of the Serbian Democratic Party have certain areas under their control and are holding them with the consent of the Yugoslav People's Army. That sounds like a complaint about the conduct of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please let me see that in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll find it for you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I'm looking for the text, Mr. Bonomy, let me say the following: In Bosnia, we had most of the Yugoslav military industry belonging to all the republics of Yugoslavia. Much of this was held by the Muslims and the Muslim units. It was under their control. The JNA did not intervene even there in order to lift the siege of those military facilities and retake them. There were quite a few accusations to the effect that the JNA left weapons for the Serbs. I can assert that the JNA left weapons to all the ethnic groups in areas from which it withdrew, for the simple reason that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's the reference to paramilitary units of the Serbian Democratic Party having all those areas under their control. That's -- I think that is what should be commented on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Plus it's the -- it's the part after that. "They're holding them with the consent of the Yugoslav People's Army." I understood you to say that Izetbegovic had no complaint to make about the army, but I was suggesting to you that that sounds like a complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 33, the second passage in Alija Izetbegovic's speech.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it now. "So who is attacking whom ..." is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Mr. Bonomy was quoting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "So who is attacking whom I do not know, but the result is such that at the moment paramilitary units of the Serbian Democratic Party have all those areas under their control. They're holding them with the consent of the Yugoslav People's Army." What I can say, Mr. Bonomy, is that the entire civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was in essence a war between three ethnic communities; Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. It was war for territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is much more specific than that, Mr. Kostic. It was simply to ask you if that was a complaint that Izetbegovic actually made, because you gave an answer a short time ago that he had no complaints to make about the Yugoslav army's conduct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I don't see this as a complaint, because the JNA did not enter into any armed clashes either with the Muslim formations or the Serb formations. It's well known that the Serbian Democratic Army -- Party had its armed units and its Territorial Defence there even before we withdrew the JNA from Bosnia. So I did not see this as a complaint against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the more so as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the JNA that they took only a month previously on the day when the independence of BH was declared?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A month previously the Presidency called on the paramilitary formations of the Muslim and Croat army to lay siege to all the JNA barracks on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was done and acted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the composition of that Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina - and I will use the correct term that Mr. Robinson used - was in its reduced composition; that is, there were no representatives of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 4th of May, you issued a decision that all units of the JNA, which was now the Yugoslav army, should leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did the armed formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina permit the army to withdraw without obstruction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. In that period while the JNA was withdrawing, we saw the most monstrous crimes committed against members of the JNA on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the attack on the JNA column in Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo on the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, General Kukanjac detained Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on his -- when he was on his way back from the Lisbon conference. They took him to the barracks in Lukavica, the JNA barracks, and during those negotiations it was agreed that the siege and encirclement in which the army command was being held by the Muslim forces should be lifted so that the command could pull out of Sarajevo. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and General Kukanjac were in that column together. I think that the UNPROFOR representative was also there, the representative for Bosnia, but the Muslim paramilitary formations did not stick to the agreement. Mr. Izetbegovic was released and allowed to go to the Presidency, and then the Muslim units cut off the column in Dobrovoljacka Street and, according to the information I had then, under the direct command of Ejub Ganic, they slaughtered the column which was not in a combat disposition. The troops were in trucks, ready for withdrawal from Sarajevo, and several soldiers and officers of the JNA were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened when the JNA was withdrawing from Tuzla on the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An even worse crime occurred with even more victims on the side of the JNA. While withdrawing pursuant to a decision by the Presidency from the Husinjska Buna barracks of the JNA in Tuzla, the army was ready to move in a column with trucks, and soldiers sitting on the tarpaulins, not posing any danger to their surroundings; however, they were ambushed and slaughtered by the Muslim forces, although they were retreating and were not able to offer resistance. According to information provided by the then command of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, about 160 members of the JNA were killed on that occasion. There was bestial behaviour. Soldiers were set alight like torches. Even wounded men were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was the 4th of May decision. The army was pulling out, the part that was from Serbia and Montenegro, but when was the army of Republika Srpska formed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska was formed on the 15th of May, 1992, or exactly one month after the BH army was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the Muslim army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when did you say that was established?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a month after that army was formed, the Republika Srpska army was established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was one army formed, the other army formed a month later. What about the members of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did they join up with the newly formed armies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did for the most part. The officers and the soldiers and the men, they all joined one or the other army. For example, Mr. Ratko Mladic was a Serb from Bosnia, and he joined the Serbian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina and was appointed commander, that is to say the army of Republika Srpska. Others, for example, other generals and high-ranking officers who were also in the Yugoslav People's Army joined up with the Muslim army or, rather, the Bosnian and Croatian coalition, or the Muslim army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Sefer Halilovic is an example. If I'm not mistaken, I think he was even the army's commander. Sefer Halilovic, Rasim Delic, Jovo Divjak, for example, who was a Serb ethnically but he joined the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. So these were all officers who had previously been officers in the Yugoslav People's Army and later up took up the top posts in one or the other army. Even in the 3rd Army, for example, and the example is that Nojko Marinovic was a high-ranking officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. Later on he came to be the commander of the Defence of Dubrovnik, just to quote another example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With that proviso and difference that Mladic was from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic was commander of the Muslim army but he was from Serbia. We're not going to dwell on Alija Izetbegovic now, but just tell us one thing: Were there any consequences? Did this produce any consequences to which the Presidency reacted, apart from what you have described to us, that is to say the massacre of the military column in Dobrovoljacka Street and so on. Did that produce any consequences?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did produce fairly significant consequences with regard to the cadres' status. The Presidency assessed that the way in which the agreement was realised, the agreement to pull out the command of the JNA from Sarajevo and to cut across the column in Dobrovoljacka Street and the casualties that ensued, along with the fact that Alija was nonetheless released and he left without an agreement being reached and without the Marshal Tito barracks being deblocked, where we had cadets living, we in the Presidency at the time considered that this was a move, without entering into the details and anybody who was to blame or the mistakes that were made, we considered that this upset the image and -- of the high-ranking officer cadre, and the Presidency made the decision that General Kukanjac should be replaced from his duties. And during the entire operation, General Blagoje Adzic was informed of the situation and kept abreast of it, and he was rather uncritical and supported General Kukanjac and tendered his own resignation, which we accepted, so that Blagoje Adzic stepped down too. He tendered his resignation and to all intents and purposes was pensioned off at the beginning of May. It was the 7th or 8th of May, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about the involvement of the armed forces of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, before that time and during those months? What was their involvement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that the basic intention of the Croatian leadership was to transfer the flames of war to its neighbouring territory; Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia, to have the conflict spill over. Its attempts to have it spill over into Serbia and Montenegro did not succeed but very soon the flames of war spread to Bosnia engulfed Bosnia.
