It was easier for them to do that because Western Herzegovina was populated exclusively by Croat inhabitants almost, and before Bosnia was recognised as an independent and sovereign state, for a long time people lived under conditions that prevailed the same as prevailed in Croatia: They had Croatian money circulating, they had Croatian signs and emblems put up. And in Posavina to the north of Bosnia, where the population was also predominantly ethnic Croats, the Croatian leadership succeeded in extending the flames of war to that area and to involve and engage its army in Bosnia as well. And we had to intervene as the Presidency because we knew that at the time on the territory of Bosnia there were about 40.000 Croatian soldiers, members of the Croatian army. So not Croats from Bosnia but members of the Croatian armed forces from the territory of Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, Professor Kostic, in paragraph 79 of the Bosnian indictment, it says: "On the 15th of May, 1992 the United Nations Security Council in its Resolution number 752 demanded that all interference from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina by units of the JNA cease immediately and that those units either be withdrawn, be subjected to the authority of the government of the Republic, or be disbanded and disarmed." Is that what Resolution 752 called for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is only part of what Resolution 752 called for. What you've just quoted to us omits stating that in that same Resolution the same request and conclusion was made and referred to members of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the need for their withdrawal from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the members of various paramilitary units. And another thing that was omitted was to emphasise that in the preamble to the Resolution it was stated that the Presidency of the SFRY or, rather, the FRY had already taken the decision to withdraw the JNA units from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this is what it says: Resolution 752 states the following: "Having considered [In English] the announcement in Belgrade the 4th of May, 1992, described in report of Secretary-General 12th of May concerning the withdrawal of Yugoslav People's Army personnel from republics other than Serbia and Montenegro and the renunciation of authority over those who remain." [Interpretation] And then point 3, paragraph 3 with regard to what you say, which is not contained in paragraph 79 of the indictment because it just refers to the JNA to leave and it had already decided to leave and was leaving: "[In English] Also demands that all forms of interference from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, including by units of the Yugoslav People's Army as well as elements of the Croatian army, cease immediately ..." [Interpretation] Point 4: "[In English] Demands also that those units of the Yugoslav People's Army and elements of Croatian army now in Bosnia-Herzegovina must either be withdrawn, or be subject to the authority of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So what is the point that you wish the witness to make about the differences between that paragraph in the indictment and Resolution 752?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, had a decision already been taken -- well, the JNA was pulling out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but did anybody take the decision that the Croatian army should enter or leave Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what is the sense of sending in mid-June 1992 by the Presidency of the SFRY a memorandum to General-Secretary Boutros-Ghali on the involvement of Croatia, Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina? The memorandum is to be found in tab 56 otherwise. It is in Serbian, which was published -- the text was published in its integrity by the mass media or, rather, the daily press. It is Wednesday, the 17th of June, 1992, and the translation is there. It is a memorandum by the Yugoslav Presidency on the involvement of Croatia in BH.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the memorandum was sent out by the Presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The contents of that memorandum in full corresponds to a report by the UN Secretary-General, and of course although to all intents and purposes the process of the JNA's withdrawal was being completed from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 27th of April we had already constituted the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and we were highly interested in seeing that in our environment, immediate environment, which meant in Bosnia-Herzegovina, too, that a peace be established and a peaceful settlement to the crisis found. At the time, we appraised the situation and thought that no peaceful solution could be found and a political settlement to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina could be found if on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an internationally already recognised state which had already become a member of the United Nations, if on the territory of that state there were 40.000 soldiers belonging to another independent state, and in this particular instance the Croatian army in Croatian state. So we considered that it would be in order to have all the armies pull out. Not only the JNA but also the Croatian army withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina and only when that had been done were conditions ripe to have the three ethnic groups find a peaceful settlement to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. We're not going to dwell on that, but what are the main issues raised in the memorandum? The military involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find the text of the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's in tab 56.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Well, another issue was -- actually, we have Croatia's military engagement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the arming of the Croatian and Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although at that time there was an embargo in full force with respect to armaments, and that was one that was brought in by the international community, and it held true for the whole of Yugoslavia, and I think that some prominent international leaders took note of that as well as the UN Secretary-General. They said that independently of the embargo, there was still weapons imports going on unimpeded, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the memorandum also addresses the issue of military and police training and the infiltration of sabotage terrorist groups and also the civilian suffering and civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there any reply from the Secretary-General to this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I recall, no, there was not. And I have to say that we wrote to them several times. But we weren't used to getting answers from them, responses to our letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just before we move on, perhaps we'll find a part of the answer -- not to the letter but an answer to the situation as such in a report by Boutros-Ghali dated the 30th of May, 1992, but before we go on to that, take a look at page 2 of this edition of the Politika newspaper and tell us whether it lists in great detail the Croatian military formations on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have eight -- the 108th, 120 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down and give us a reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter is asking you to speak more slowly and to provide a reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading from tab 56. It is a -- the document is the memorandum of the Presidency of Yugoslavia on Croatian engagement in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is the second column on page 2. Will you read it. "A. North-east Bosnia --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A. North-east Bosnia, five to six brigades of the Croatian army there: The 108th, 124th, 103rd and 139th Brigade, and parts of the 101st, 109th and 131st Brigade, making a total of 10 to 20.000 men. "B. Western Herzegovina and the Neretva River valley, ten brigades there: The 4th, the 115th, the 126th, the 142nd, the 155th and the 156th, the 119th, the 114th, 110th, and 116th Brigade of the Croatian army, totalling about 20.000 men." As I said, totalling about 20.000 men. "C. Sector Livno, Duvno and Sujica, three brigades of the Croatian army: The 106th, 109th, and parts of the 115th Brigades of the Croatian army, and the 1st and 4th ZNG - Croatian National Guards - Brigades, a total of 5 to 7.000 men. "D. Territory of Eastern Herzegovina, three brigades of the Croatian army: 113th, 114th, and 158th Brigade of the Croatian army, and the Plavi Grom and Pustinjska Lisica armoured units. Part of these forces is engaged in the wide area of Dubrovnik. The carrying out of these forces' offensives is in progress, a component of which is the artillery shelling of Trebinje and Nevesinje."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Trebinje and Nevesinje, what was the composition, ethnic composition there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly Serbian inhabitants. They are towns in Herzegovina predominantly populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did we see prior reference to members of these units who were taken prisoner, to they were as well as a number of other details about individuals taken captive from various brigades?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, we will look at this report by Boutros Boutros-Ghali on the 30th of May, 1992. Are you familiar with the contents of that report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are the basic elements of that report those that coincide with what you in the Presidency knew?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 83, Security Council Resolution 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's the 30th of May. And I will only ask you whether the basic elements of that report coincide with what you knew as vice-president of the Federal Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated in the report made by Secretary-General of the United Nations not only coincided with our knowledge but coincided to a great extent with what we stated in our memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will only quote a few points and you will tell me whether they coincide. Paragraph 5: "The bulk of the JNA personnel [In English] who were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina where citizens of that Republic and were not therefore covered by the Belgrade authorities decision of 4th of May to withdraw JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them appear to have joined the army of so-called 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.' Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is under the political control of the Presidency of that Republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there." [Interpretation] Is that the same description as what you have just stated about the course of events during the retreat and everything that was happening at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same description, and it's what I said to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic in Skopje as to what they will be faced with during the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to say anything about units of the Croatian army, or does that come later?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In point 10, Mr. Bonomy: "[In English] As regards the withdrawal of the elements of the Croatian army now in Bosnia, information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of Croatian army personnel, in uniform, operating within, and as a part of, military formation in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it goes on to say that Croatian authorities consistently take the position that Croatian soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina have left the Croatian army and are not subject to their authority, but it says: "International observers do not, however, doubt [In English] that portions of Bosnia-Herzegovina are under control of Croatian military units, whether belonging to the local Territorial Defence, to paramilitary group, or to the Croatian army." [Interpretation] So it is stated here. Now, in point 8, it is stated: "Uncertainty about who exercises political control over the Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina has further complicated the situation. [In English] The Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency had initially been reluctant to engage in talks on these and other issues with the leadership of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina' and insisted upon direct talks with Belgrade authorities instead." [Interpretation] Those Belgrade authorities mean you and Izetbegovic talking on the 26th of April, and we saw the result. "Senior JNA representative ... General Nedeljko Boskovic, has conducted discussions ... but it has become clear that his word is not binding on the commander of the army of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina,' General Mladic. [In English] Indeed, as indicated in paragraph 6(b) above, Serb irregulars attacked a JNA convoy withdrawing from barracks at Sarajevo on 28 May under arrangement negotiation by General Boskovic. It also appears that the heavy shelling of Sarajevo on the night of 28/29 May took place on the orders of General Mladic in direct contravention of instructions issued by General Boskovic and the JNA leadership in Belgrade." [Interpretation] Are you aware about this point that withdrawing convoys were being stopped?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They not only stopped the convoys, but I have to say they made it difficult for us to negotiate with the Muslim side the lifting of the siege from army barracks. The army of the Muslim Federation had been already established, very massively equipped, whereas the Territorial Defence of the Serb side did not have enough weaponry, and it was in their interest. They were anxious to take over the weaponry of the withdrawing JNA. And they even made it difficult to start the process of lifting the siege from the barracks, making it a condition that officers and personnel should withdraw but to leave their weapons behind. This was typical not only of Serbs but also Croats and Muslims. Everywhere where the JNA was withdrawing, people would put up roadblocks, come out en masse into the street to stop JNA convoys from withdrawing. And the JNA if it wanted to pull out its weapons as well, they had to roll over those people in tanks. And as I said, General Nedeljko Boskovic visited Sarajevo, and he reported to me in my office, saying that he was going to try to liberate the barracks that held those 300 cadets captive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now let us just look at one last thing, item 9 of the report of the UN Secretary-General. "Given the doubts that now exist about the ability of the authorities in Belgrade [In English] to influence General Mladic, who has left JNA, efforts have been made by UNPROFOR to appeal to him directly as well as through the political leadership of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.' As result of these efforts, General Mladic agreed on 30 May to stop the bombardment of Sarajevo. While it is my hope that the shelling of the city will not be resumed, it is also clear that the emergence of General Mladic and the forces under his command as independent actors apparently beyond the control of JNA greatly complicates the issues raised in paragraph 4 of Security Council Resolution 752. President Izetbegovic has recently indicated to senior UNPROFOR officers at Sarajevo his willingness to deal with General Mladic but not with the political leadership of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.'" [Interpretation] Do you know anything about this and about Izetbegovic's position that he should independently negotiate with Mladic, that he did not accept a talk with Radovan Karadzic who was at that time the president of what was then called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, otherwise his rejection of political contacts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What we read in the report by UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali of the 30th of May, is that approximately the same thing that you knew in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in my view it's an objective assessment of the situation in Bosnia. That's one. And second, later on, when I had already retired from the Presidency, various solutions were sought for the situation for Bosnia in Belgrade whereas that should have been done in Sarajevo. Instead of -- in fact, I -- I already said we have -- we had pulled out all the JNA on the 19th of May, and we publicly stated that we have no longer any responsibility or any powers over the remaining armed forces in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you not refer to this report in the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This one? I remember a report you referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This report was admitted as D91.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was now trying to establish the relationship between what the Presidency wrote in their memorandum and what Mr. Kostic discussed with Mr. Izetbegovic, and I compared all of that to what the Secretary-General chose to put in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you consider this to be an important part of your case relating to the question of your responsibility, individual responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, you were telling me yesterday that I should go into specific details, and you see that Mr. Kostic, even while he occupied his post at the top of the whole SFRY, didn't know anything about those details. So how could I, who was only President of Serbia, know about these details, apart from conducting an investigation on the scale that the people on the opposite side are carrying out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No doubt we will have some assurance as to the significance of this report in the final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, it says that the joint criminal enterprise existed from the 1st of August, 1991, until the 31st December, 1995, and I am now going to ask you -- in fact, paragraph 47 says the entire time to which this indictment refers there was a state of international armed conflict and partial occupation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When was the independence of Bosnia proclaimed? When was it recognised by some countries of the European Union? When did the referendum of the Bosnian people take place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina took place on the 29th of February, 1992. I think. The independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed and simultaneously recognised on the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 6th of April is the anniversary of the bombing of Belgrade by Hitler in 1941.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you as a participant in this joint criminal enterprise, how do you view the allegation that there was an international armed conflict and partial occupation in Bosnia for all of eight months prior to the proclamation of Bosnian independence and prior to the outbreak of the war in that republic? Maybe you as participant in this joint criminal enterprise can see it more clearly than a regular observer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the question that was just asked, that's a question to answer for the Judges in their findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to say, tell the witness: Confine your answer to issues of fact that will assist the Chamber in determining the question of an international armed conflict. You're not to pass judgement on that yourself, but you can provide information which is relevant to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not a lawyer, after all, and I don't feel called upon, even if the Court allowed me to make such assessments, but from all that we have discussed so far regarding the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I can only recall all the talks and all the agreements we had reached regarding the status of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina, our talks with Mr. Izetbegovic concerning the withdrawal of JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the fact that after the 19th of May we didn't have a single soldier left there. What remained were three armies, three peoples, each led by their own leadership and despite all the attempts to find a peaceful solution, a fierce war started raging. That's one part of the answer. Second, I really cannot explain, but the authors of the indictment might be able to, how come that this large number of participants in the joint criminal enterprise from August 1991 until 1995 is possible if we recall that Mr. Veljko Kadijevic, who is also mentioned, resigned on the 8th of January, 1992, and went straight to be hospitalised. On the 8th of May, 1992, Blagoje Adzic submitted his resignation. I as vice-president of the Federal Presidency handed over my duties to the first elected president of Yugoslavia on the 15th of June and I completely retired from political life. Those are just some details that I would like to recall, and maybe the Prosecution can explain our participation in the JCE and what it consists of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here is what it consists of: You are not on trial here, nor is Kadijevic. It says here in paragraph 28: "Generals Blagoje Adzic and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Generals Veljko Kadijevic and Blagoje Adzic, who directed and supervised the JNA forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were in constant communication and consultation with the accused." Now, I want to ask you: Did Kadijevic and Adzic lead the forces in Bosnia and did they supervise them when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic couldn't have been in charge of the forces in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is this evident, the person who consulted me was retired when the war broke out in Bosnia. Did I participate in this and issue instructions to someone who was retired, a pensioner?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a lot of nonsense being reiterated here again and again. We've already seen it in the Croatia indictment. So I see no reason to go into it yet again. All the more so as it is evident here that with regard to events in Bosnia, some of these highest-ranking people from the JNA had already retired or resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But here they are mentioned as a link to me. So according to what is stated here, I was supposed to have influenced -- influenced this, that is the situation in Bosnia, through pensioners such as Kadijevic and Adzic. We're talking about issues of fact here, not law.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert whether you ever had any communication with Kadijevic and Adzic, but if we take into account the statement made by General Vasiljevic, who knew about all these links better than I did and who stated as a Prosecution witness that you could not influence General Kadijevic even while he was active and while he was the federal secretary of defence, so how could you have influenced him after he retired and after he was admitted to hospital? I myself visited him in hospital, so how could you have influenced the events in Bosnia through him I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't dwell any longer on this. Have you read the Bosnia indictment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you established to what extent it corresponds to the Croatia indictment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's almost cut and paste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you find a single statement here that might be linked to any activities of the President of Serbia - that is, me - anything that indicates a connection between the leadership of Serbia and my activities and these events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question is far too wide. I'm not allowing it. I told you to ask questions that were focussed and specific.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll put a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about my activities regarding the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's just as wide. We'll get a one-hour lecture from the professor. You have to be -- you have to be -- don't answer that. Don't answer that question. Mr. Milosevic is to be more focused in his questions, and he knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which of my activities linked to Bosnia and Herzegovina are you aware of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period I was in the Presidency, that is until the 15th of June, what you did was to use your political authority to advocate a peaceful solution and the acceptance of the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my examination-in-chief, Mr. Robinson, even before I had planned it, in order not to go through the same charges that are found in the Bosnia as well as in the Croatia indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just one administrative question, more or less, about the tabs that we talked about. I assume they will all be admitted, however, I would have an objection against admitting this video clip, this second one with this huge military whatever one would call it, because we don't have no reference to the date or the purpose on what we are really seeing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit the other documents but not the video clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the second video clip. The statement by the Reis-Ul-Ulema, who says it's God's order that jihad be waged, will you exhibit that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will exhibit that one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you understand, then, that what he says has to do with the Mujahedin Brigade being reviewed by Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But nobody could see anything on that clip, Mr. Milosevic. It wasn't -- it wasn't intelligible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And there was no translation, at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We couldn't make any sense of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's mostly shouting in the Arabic language of a religious nature, a militant religious nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But how are we to know that? You are not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have the tape examined and then I will tender it once again. Very well. Thank you. I thought you could distinguish between the Arabic language and other languages, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. The witness was not able to see it, and we skipped that part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that the witness's monitor wasn't working. That's not something I can control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, during your testimony, you commented on several pages, paragraphs of the Croatia indictment. You know it well; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You know that it deals with crimes committed between the 1st of August, 1991, until June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So -- so, Mr. Kostic, you know that the population figures that you gave us here comparing the data from 1991 with the data of 2001 do not assist this Court. It cannot assist this Court. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. How can they not be of assistance? The information I provided about the population figures can certainly be of assistance to the Court. We can view the information differently, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what this information includes are actually the results of the Operation Storm and the Operation Flash, these Croat offensives, and this is what really brought about this big discrepancy in relation to the Serb population. That's a fact, is it not? And that's 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my testimony we spoke about the atmosphere that prevailed on the territory of Croatia from the very first day. I'm referring to the areas with the majority Serb population. And it seems to me that we have very successfully explained how the beginning of armed conflicts came about on Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Let me stop you here, Mr. Kostic. Mr. Kostic, these figures that you gave to the Judges include the changes in population in 1995, do they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They include all the changes from 1991 to 2001. All the changes. That's the final result of everything that happened in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you are aware, and you have commented on this, that you are in paragraphs 7 and 10 of the Croatia indictment mentioned as a member of the joint criminal enterprise and you are considered to be responsible for the crimes charged in Croatia and also partly in Bosnia. You are aware of this, are you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, that I feel responsible for any crimes. I expect you to tell me today what crimes those might be for which I might be held responsible, but I said I never felt responsible for any crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That was not my question. I would really ask you to listen to what I'm asking. I asked you that you in this indictment are mentioned to be responsible for these crimes as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. That's what you yourself said.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only ask to be allowed to establish the difference between what you said now and your first question. I never for a moment stated that I felt responsible or guilty of the crimes mentioned in the indictment. I did say, however, that in that period I was vice-president of the Presidency of the SFRY, and I also said during my testimony that all decisions that we as the Presidency of the SFRY issued, both in our full and in our reduced composition, were aimed at finding a peaceful solution to the political crisis and not towards war. If you insist on this --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let's stop here. It seems that you don't want to understand my question. Given the actions of the JNA, Mr. Milosevic himself said something, and I quote now from transcript 47771 of the 1st of February, this -- at the beginning of the cross -- of the examination-in-chief: "All these events that are mentioned here in the indictment were taking place up until mid-1992. And here we have a witness who was the vice-president of the Presidency, which was the Supreme Commander of that army which had allegedly committed certain things. So that absolutely does not mean that the crimes happened there, the ones mentioned in the indictment. But it does show who had competency and power and authority at that time ..." To put it simple, Mr. Kostic, Mr. Milosevic is basically saying if the JNA committed crimes, it's not his responsibility but yours, Mr. Kostic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that we discussed, I was the vice-president of the Presidency, which was the Supreme Command. As the Supreme Command, we had authority over the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you would be the one responsible, then, for the crimes charged?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were such crimes, then I might be held responsible for them, but I neither mentioned those crimes nor did I accept any claim from the indictment that the JNA committed such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you know the place Sarvas?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would like to refer you to the atlas. It's Exhibit 336, and we perhaps can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's page 23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you know the place Sarvas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never been there but I have heard the name of that place from that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's south or -- let's say it's south of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you find it, Witness? Do you see it here? It's south-east from Osijek, it's close to Aljmas, Erdut, Dalj, in Eastern Slavonia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You know that in Dalj and Sarvas clashes occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We actually dealt with an exhibit, a Defence exhibit. It's Defence Exhibit 333, tab 26, from the 8th of August, 1991, where there was a Presidency session dealing with this; right? It mentions that there should be a commission for monitoring cease-fire and that they should have -- they should inquire on what happened in Sarvas and Dalj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the 13th of August, the Presidency dealt again with this issue of what happened in Dalj, Sarvas, and Lovinac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we dealt with that. I don't recall every detail, but I do know we dealt with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's actually Exhibit 330, tab 11. It's the draft minutes of this Presidency session of 13 of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I don't think I need to put it to you, Mr. Kostic, because you know about it, and I only want to relate to one point, because it says in this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff has to show the witness the document. He cannot remember something that happened 15 years ago and just be told, "You know about this." He has to be able to see the document in order to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't have draft minutes in the Presidency. We only had minutes. What kind of draft minutes are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can it be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to make it short because the witness remembered this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the second page --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be passed to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the 133rd session of the Presidency of 13 August 1991, and in the first -- in the preamble, more to speak, above the agenda, it says that you were present as well. Under point 1 -- if you look at the next page, there is point 1, and at the end of point 1, it says the following: "The SFRY Presidency decided to ask the Federal Executive Council to form a mixed expert commission for investigating the facts regarding the events in the villages of Dalj, Sarvas, and Lovinac in Croatia and then inform the public." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really recall the details, but as we see here, it was agreed that Vasil Tupurkovski and Bogic Bogicevic should have talks with the leadership of Slovenia. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the commission that were supposed to look into the events in Dalj, Sarvas, and Lovinac. Do you recall that now when you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall about this particular commission. What I can say is that we formed such commissions more than once. There was another commission, a state commission of which I was the chairman when Mr. Mesic walked out of the session because I was elected chairman of that state commission. As for this commission here, I really don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that there were clashes in Dalj, Sarvas, and Lovinac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just there, in many other places too, but there also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We actually heard witnesses -- witness evidence on the events in these three places, and I would like to quote from a witness statement of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C57 and Exhibit 607, tab 1. As this is an exhibit under seal, I would rather not give it to the witness but simply read from it the part that were -- are not under seal. Is that something we could agree upon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This witness, Mr. Kostic, speaks about -- in paragraph 29 of his witness statement, speaks about capturing Aljmas and the destruction of the Catholic church in Aljmas, and I cannot read to you the full paragraph because I can only read from the public version. It says: "In early September --" and then there is something I cannot talk about. He speaks about the unit that was tasked with attacking Sarvas. That's what the witness mentioned in paragraph 29. He also mentioned attacks on Aljmas. He says in paragraph 30: "Aljmas was completely deserted save for a dozen elderly people and a few married couples." In paragraph 31 this witness speaks about the church of Aljmas being mined by Arkan's volunteers. And then he speaks about the capturing of Sarvas. In paragraph 34, he says: "I saw that the village was completely deserted and heavily damaged by tanks and artillery fire. I had assumed this would be the case because fire had been opened at the village from tanks throughout the day." And finally, in paragraph 88, the witness told us that: "In spring of 1992, Serbs from Western Slavonia started settling in the area where I was located. They moved into Croatian houses in Aljmas and Sarvas and also in Erdut, and at the same time the names of the villages were changed and new Cyrillic signs were put up at the entrances to the villages. So Aljmas was renamed Papuk Dolina, and Sarvas became Jelenovo." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, don't make me laugh. Do I remember Aljmas and Dalj and Sarvas, in the way you're putting your question. Why didn't you investigate who it was that fired the shots and destroyed the Catholic church? How would I know about these details you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, stop. I just asked you a simple question, do you remember Sarvas, because I felt you should because you wrote about Sarvas in your book, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'll tell you what I wrote about Sarvas. You don't have to ask me about it, I can tell you verbatim what I wrote about it right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my book, I wrote about Sarvas. You see, we had concluded cease-fires so many times, and throughout my testimony I kept affirming that every cease-fire was always violated by Croatian paramilitary formations. I often had occasion, and I mentioned this in my book, through television and radio --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I'll let you answer to my question and the question related to Sarvas. You do not need to repeat all the things that you said in the examination-in-chief. Just concentrate on what your book said on Sarvas, if you remember. Otherwise, I'll put it in front of you. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do as the Prosecutor has intimated. Otherwise, we can just have the book placed on the ELMO. Why don't you do that, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I think it's easier to put it on the ELMO. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's time for the break, so we'll get back to that in 20 minutes. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we discover what the witness wrote about Sarvas, let me just clarify the exhibits. We have admitted tabs 32, 5, and 56. Tabs 84, 62, 81 and 83, which were also dealt with by the accused, had already been admitted as exhibits and therefore will not be readmitted. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear you mention tab 5. That was the audio recording of the Izetbegovic meeting, Izetbegovic-Kostic meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the transcript. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we -- you have now an excerpt from your book, "1991 Not To Be Forgotten" in front of you, page 101. I think everybody has now also the translation, and it says here on this page, it says here: "I first met with General Zivota Panic, 1st Army Commander, and a group of his associates, when opening the Agricultural Fair in Novi Sad on 4 September 1991. Radio and television were reporting daily on Croatian paramilitaries from Sarvas threatening members of the JNA who were placed as a buffer zone to prevent international conflicts. On that occasion, I asked them, 'Is that Sarvas so well fortified that you couldn't take it and chase away those who are threatening you daily?' And they replied that they could mop that up in a single afternoon but that they should not because of a cease-fire that had been signed and because of a strict order of the General Staff to observe the cease-fire. 'If I were you, I told them, I would tolerate the enemy breaching the cease-fire once, even twice or three times, but after that I would silence them, and I would not wait for authorisation if the lives of our soldiers were threatened.' "On the following week, the Croatian paramilitaries were chased away from Sarvas, but I never found out if our conversation had influenced them taking that action ..." Do you remember that conversation with General Panic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness. Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that well. The photocopy of the text is precisely as it is written in my book.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender this section of the book. I don't know how to do it. The book -- the book has already -- it's tab 72, but just the parts that Mr. Milosevic had provided. I wonder whether we should keep it as tab 72 or whether it should be now a Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Part of tab 72, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- before you move on, my tab 72 has nothing in it. Are you saying we already have parts of this book?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My understanding is that only those parts that were translated here in -- here in the courtroom are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, as you have -- as this book shows, you were fully aware of the events in that region Sarvas, and as a member of the Presidency you actually should; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what was going on in Sarvas. Had I known, I would not have asked General Panic What's going on in Sarvas? And do you allow paramilitaries illegal, irregular members of the Croatian army to jeopardise the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, the only constitutional armed forces. Had I had the details about Sarvas, I wouldn't have asked General Panic that. And everything we've read out here deserves additional comment in the following sense: That if a truce had been agreed and one of the parties fails to respect that truce, the agreement, and violates it once, twice, three times, four times, then in that case the units of the regular army need not wait for anybody's orders to step in in self-defence. They should and can undertake activities to protect their own lives. And one of the things that I have noticed and one of my observations that you could have found in the book that you're quoting from, although I'm not highly trained -- a highly trained military person, I was just a reserve major in the Yugoslav People's Army, nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please concentrate on short answers. I asked you whether you were -- according to this, you seemed to be quite informed about the region, and you say no, you weren't. That's actually the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you allow me to finish my train of thought? It's not proper of you to interrupt my train of thought if you've already asked me a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, she can. She can stop you if you're not answering the question, but all of that is subject to the ultimate control of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: According to your book, it sounds as if you wanted Sarvas to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to know where you read that from, because the witness told us more than once in his examination-in-chief that he was the one in the leadership that thought the army should be unblocking the various barracks where the -- their colleagues were held, and that seemed to me a perfectly reasonable approach to take. In fact, I think I may have asked a question about it. Now, what is it that you say in here suggests that he wanted to attack civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't say that he wanted to attack civilians. I'm sorry. I just -- I said it sounds as if he wanted Sarvas to be attacked, the place. I didn't say something about civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, where do you read that in here? It seems to be the paramilitaries he wants to be attacked, to be removed from the blockage they were causing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I read it actually from the sentence: "If I were you, I would remove --" the sentence that I quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But only after they have breached the cease-fire three times, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. I think I move on now. I made my point. But I've just -- my colleagues just told me that when I spoke with the witness about Defence Exhibit D333, tab 28, that's the session of the Presidency of the 8th of August, 1991. I was just told by my colleagues that it is actually not tendered. Mr. Milosevic did not tender it, but I would -- oh, I'm sorry, tab 26. I misspoke. Tab 26. The Prosecution would like to tender it, and perhaps we put it to the witness as -- yes. We should put it to the witness so that I can ask you one more question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let the document be passed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness should have the Cyrillic, and on the ELMO we should have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would like you to -- to turn to point 4 in this document, where it says: "At 1300 hours today members of the SFRY Presidency commission and three representatives, each of the government of the Republic of Croatia and the Serbian people of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't have that. I haven't got the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 26. Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just quoting from point 4 on this document where there is the reference to the commission, and I was quoting who participated here, and it says here: "... will visit the villages of Dalj and Sarvas to resolve the pressing issues there. A working group formed by the Federal Executive Council and representatives of Osijek Municipal Assembly will also participate in the work." And in the following paragraph, it says here: "Persons who have been detained according to lists previously submitted to the commission are to be released by 1800 hours today and activities intended to determine the identities of missing persons are to be continued." Mr. Kostic, I read from what is said here that the Presidency commission dealt with the situation and it was actually a clash that involved victims on all sides or detained people on all sides. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document, the one you quoted from, all I can see is that an initiative was taken to establish or, rather, to investigate the case, to establish a commission to investigate the case, but I don't remember whether there was a commission report or what its contents were. I can only assume that since we're dealing with the month of August here, that it was the interim period which resulted in the complete blockade of the Presidency, when the Presidency was no longer able to meet. It was at an impasse. So that I don't know whether the working group that was appointed, that was nominated, I can't say anything about that. All I can do is to assume that the commission worked within the commission of the federal government. But I don't remember that we received a report from the commission at the Presidency at all about the results of its work, what the findings were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would probably be clearer if the first paragraph were read out, where you can see who the commission was, the Presidency commission, led by Vasil Tupurkovski and Bogic Bogicevic, and who the members were, then it would be clearer what this was about, because it is about the Presidency working commission, and then we would know what it was all about. So, first of all we have to establish who and then what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That can be easily read from the document, and I don't think we need to go into these details. I will come, actually later on, when we discuss crimes, I will come back to this commission. There is no need to dwell on this now any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, as a member of the Presidency and later even more so in your function as the vice-president of the Rump Presidency or, as you call it, reduced Presidency, you were part of the body that controlled and directed the actions of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency was a collective Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When I say "you," I just mean this collective body; I don't mean you only alone. And throughout your tenure in the Presidency, the JNA acted on your orders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might just be allowed to add -- or to explain, rather. The division of competencies between the Presidency of the Supreme Command and the power of the staff of the Supreme Command as a professional organ was precisely determined. So the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You have already addressed this issue. We don't have to repeat this. During the second day of your testimony, when you discussed Defence Exhibit D333, tab 69, that's Kadijevic's statement of the 6th of July 1991 on peace and not war is in the interest of all, you confirmed with Mr. Milosevic that the army had never done anything on its own initiative, its constitutional powers and the decisions of the relevant federal organs, in particular the Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony, I said that the Yugoslav People's Army was very restrained in its conduct and that it respected the Presidency as being the Supreme Command, but I also reminded you of the division of powers, because the Presidency as the Supreme Command did not have within its competencies and powers, for example, orders -- it wasn't the body that was there to decide how the units of the JNA people's army would be deployed and on what territory and so on. That came under the powers of the General Staff, the professional organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, my colleague just reminded me that this -- we wanted this tab 69 to be admitted as ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. I'm advised that it's tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's tab 26, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 26, yes. We'll admit tab 26. 69 is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, as you said, you were a part of the Supreme Command of the JNA. That means that you would be to a high degree responsible if this Court would establish that the JNA and its subordinate forces committed crimes in Croatia and until June 1992 in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, aren't you doing what you advised Mr. Milosevic not to do, asking the -- asking questions that are ultimately matters for the Chamber? It's not for him to say whether he would be legally responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I have to reformulate this -- this question. I didn't want to make him that -- I didn't want him to make a finding.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Given that situation, you have a very strong interest in the outcome of the trial; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am interested in having the real truth established. And you haven't made any great efforts to arrive at the real truth. And I have come here principally to assist the Trial Chamber in establishing the truth and the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I put to you if crimes would be established here, you would -- it would have an impact on you as a person and your own responsibility. So you did not come here to help this Court to come to the truth but, rather, exonerate yourself and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You spoke about the events in Plitvice and Pakrac. This Court has heard evidence in relation to what happened in Pakrac. Would you agree with me that the accounts of what happened in Plitvice and Pakrac are quite different, that people describe what happened different from you, in particular, Croatians? Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say where the difference lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that as far as all the details are concerned from Sarvas and Pakrac and Plitvice and other places in Croatia which existed as hotbeds of crisis, I really don't know the details of. And you can insist as much you like. You can insist I tell you the details but I don't know about the details so I can't tell you, and that's why I said it, not in any derogatory sense. If I was in the Supreme Command, I still can't know about all the details, and that's why I made a joke and said I expect that in a while you'll accuse Mr. Blair, for example, of everything that happened in London last night, for the killings and thefts and rapes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. We are not talking about Mr. Blair. I was just confirming with you that people may have different accounts about what happened in Plitvice and Pakrac, and you wouldn't really be able to tell us because you were not there; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But are you aware that in relation to the event in Pakrac, Mr. Jovic ordered the JNA to intervene without having convened a Presidency -- a Presidency session and gotten their decision? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't know about that, that Mr. Jovic did that. If he did that on his own, the question arises as to whether he needed a Presidency decision or whether he already had a Presidency decision to that effect. If --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let me interrupt you. We don't -- it was a simple question. I asked you whether you know that Mr. Jovic ordered the JNA to intervene without convening a Presidency session and you say -- your answer is you don't know that. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know that he did also order the JNA to intervene in relation to the 9th of March, 1991, demonstrations in Belgrade? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I wasn't in the Presidency, but I was informed about that as well, and as far as I know, Mr. Jovic conducted consultations with the Presidency members and got their agreement to engaging the army, as far as I know. Perhaps it wasn't a session in the plenary sense, in the plenary hall, but because the situation was urgent and the danger of civil conflicts in Belgrade, he might have consulted them by phone on the 9th of March, the other members of the Presidency, and received instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At the time of the events in Plitvice and Pakrac were you a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this mass of dates I would have to remind myself of when the Pakrac situation happened. I can't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you put that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We're talking about March 1991, and the witness was not in the Presidency. I only asked him whether he knows about these decisions, and at least he knows -- he knew about the later one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The position of the president of the SFRY Presidency in urgent situation is quite an important one; right? He could start initiative in relation to the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The function of the president of the Presidency compared to the other members of the Presidency in conditions of imminent threat of war is not different, no different than it is otherwise. What is different is that the Presidency as a collective organ can meet even if it doesn't have a simple or two-thirds majority, and can make decisions within the composition that it had met. But the president of the Presidency has no greater powers and authorisations in conditions of an imminent threat of war than he does in a normal situation as president of the collective organ, whether as head of state -- whether the organ is head of state or the organ is the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, Mr. Borisav Jovic himself told us here when he gave testimony --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I refer here to Exhibit 596, tab 1, paragraph 60, where Mr. Jovic writes about the events in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic ordered the JNA to intervene without convening a Presidency session and without actually getting decision by the Presidency. And my only question is: At times of urgency, the president had a powerful position and could do something; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered that question. To the best of my knowledge, in extraordinary situations the president of the Presidency does not have any greater powers than under normal conditions. Now, what happened in Pakrac at the time, that was not an extraordinary situation, an emergency situation still. An extraordinary or emergency situation is only considered what happened after the 3rd of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your testimony you said that in Plitvice and Pakrac there were regular police stations manned by Serbs and that they were part of the Croatian authorities. And that's actually at transcript reference 47661 of the 25th of January this year. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having stated exactly that in Pakrac and Plitvice there were exclusively police forces, but I said that in those areas where there was a predominantly Serb majority population, that police stations did exist as part of the Croatian police, as part of the Croatian police force, and that where there was a predominantly Serb majority, in those police stations there were policemen who were the local population, and that they were predominantly Serbs. I can't answer specifically whether that was in Pakrac or Plitvice and what the situation was like in the police stations there exactly, whether there was a majority of Serb or Croat policemen. I can't say that and I don't think I claimed either one during my testimony earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were aware of the events in Knin in August 1999, and you yourself have referred to it as log revolution, and you know -- oh, sorry. I said 1999. It's 1990. Sorry. I misspoke. In 1990, the log revolution, and you know that Milan Martic and his police did not accept the Croatian authorities and had actually severed his ties with the Croatian MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you any details about it, because simply it was 1990 and I was not yet on the Presidency of the SFRY at that time. What I know is that Croatian police units and special units of the MUP of Croatia tried to penetrate the Knin area and other majority Serb areas to take over their police stations and practically disarm the local policemen, who were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I had actually asked you at that point in time when this happened, the local police stations had actually severed their ties with the Croatian MUP. You know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether they severed the ties or not. All I know is that they tried to prevent special Croatian forces and units from arriving. They tried to enter those areas and to take over power. I really don't know who severed ties.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we heard evidence to that effect that Milan Martic, as an example, rejected the new uniforms, the new flags, and the authorities in the MUP in Croatia in 1990 when there was the so-called log revolution. You claim you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Milan Martic refused uniforms or not, but what I have mentioned in my earlier evidence, and I can confirm it in front of you now, is that the Serb population in those areas simply rebelled in fear of what might happen to them. So they undertook to self-organise in those areas and publicly stated they would not recognise Croatian laws and the Croatian constitution that resulted from rejection of Yugoslav laws. They said they would abide by Yugoslav legislation instead. And I can tell you what Mr. Mesic did as president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Stop here. My question was actually quite simple, and there need not be a long history answer to that. Mr. Kostic, neither the SFRY constitution nor the Croatian constitution foresaw any parallel self-declared Serb police acting outside of the competencies of the republican police organs; right? There is no legal foundation for forming a separate police force, a Serb police force.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was not a Serb police force, a separate Serb police force. Croatian authorities, including the Croatian MUP and police, simply became renegade in rejecting the governing Yugoslav laws, and that in its turn caused the Serb population to reject the new Croatian laws. I don't think you should go on interrupting me. I wanted to say that Mr. Mesic constantly called those people in those areas Chetniks, bandits, renegades, and I kept sitting next to him and listening to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You may not like it, but you need to answer my questions, and you are not allowed to just tell whatever you like to say. Let me ask you this: You are aware --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't have to say things that you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have to answer my question, Mr. Kostic. That's all you are asked to do, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the questions as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in relation to Plitvice, was someone killed? Do you know that a Croat was actually killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know such details. I know that every such incident claimed victims, both Serbs and Croats, but I don't know these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You testified - and that's at transcript 47617, that's from the 25th of January - that when in March 1991 the military leadership suggested to the federal Presidency to introduce a state of emergency, four members were in favour of it and four were against it. And actually, Mr. Milosevic also followed this up in further questions and also spoke of this four-to-four deadlock situation. Do you remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that you made a mistake and that in fact the situation of the vote in the Presidency was actually four to three? Four opposing to introduce a state of emergency and three only in favour of it? Do you allow for that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could refresh my memory a little, because from what I remember, there were four votes against and four votes in favour. After all, that session lasted three days, and every now and then during those three days there were votings of various sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Borisav Jovic has testified in this case already, and he was a member of the Presidency at that time. Actually, in March 1991, he was its president; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he kept a diary during the events which he later, in 1995, published as the book "The Last Days of the SFRY." Do you know that book?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, but some points that relate to the period when I was in the Presidency, I read those passage carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as he wrote the book, as he told us here, he did not base it on memory but based it on his daily notes and on official minutes and other documents. You are aware of this; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can tell you about that is my impression. I read carefully that book of Mr. Jovic in the part that covers the period when I was in the Presidency and when we worked together. From what I read about that period, I arrived at the conclusion that after all, Mr. Jovic did not really keep a very precise record in the form of a diary. He probably just took notes and dated them later. I'll give you an example. In that book you are quoting from, he writes about the 15th or the 14th of July - I'm not quite certain at this point - saying that the decision to withdraw the JNA from Slovenia was adopted then. However, it is a well-known fact that that decision was passed on the 18th of July. And from that little detail, I inferred that Mr. Jovic did not really keep a tidy diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let's return to the book, and let's return what Mr. Jovic wrote in the book in relation to that Presidency session on the 12th of March, 1991, this long session of three days. And I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's an extract from Exhibit 596, tab 2, Mr. Jovic's book, and it's his entries from the 12th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kostic, it is quite a lengthy document, and I would simply draw your attention to a few particular points made here. Now I have the English. On page 2, we have Mr. Kadijevic speaking about the situation, and he says: "First that a decision be adopted immediately imposing a state of knowledge in the entire territory of the SFRY and that all normative laws in conflict with the SFRY constitution and federal laws be suspended. "Second, that a decision be adopted raising the combat readiness of the armed forces ..." And a little bit further down, he says: "Third, that the disrupted system of national defence be restored to its constitutional framework ..." That was the proposal that Mr. Kadijevic put to the Presidency at that time. Is that what you also remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that session because I wasn't on the Presidency then. I really can't talk to you about it. I can't give you any details. I know very well that that session lasted three days; on the 12th, the 14th, and the 15th. On the first day -- on day one, the proposal made by Veljko Kadijevic to the Presidency could not be accepted. There was a break in the session. And I can talk to you about it because I viewed a film from that session that was broadcast several times, and that's how I know about these things. Otherwise, not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Jovic agreed to this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's on page 257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic agreed to the proposal? Yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Mesic rejected it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tupurkovski rejected it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Bogicevic rejected it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rejected it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Riza Sapundzija rejected it? That's the representative for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
