utterances.text: That detail concerning Mr. Riza Sapundzija, I really don't know about it in any precision. I think Mr. Sapundzija had the opportunity to vote twice or three times during that session, but I really don't know the details. Since we are talking about the first day, the 12th of March, I don't know what his position was. I know that in the course of those three days, in one round of voting, as far as I remember the film, the position of Riza Sapundzija was negative. But it could have been the third day of the session, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to quote something from this text of Mr. Jovic. It's page 258 in the English, and it's actually from Mr. Nenad Bucin. That's the member from Montenegro. You have it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He says: "I do not challenge Veljko's assessment. If I were to undertake any analysis, my conclusion would probably be gloomy. As I take the floor, however, I am thinking about all the previous declarations, our total paralysis and inability - I would even say unwillingness - to arrive at decisions even in much more innocuous situations than this one now. For me, the only possibility remains acknowledging that we as a Presidency are not in a position to lead this country ..." Actually, this is not agreeing to -- he is not agreeing here to imposition of a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how I understood Mr. Bucin's position. My personal opinion, although I didn't attend the session but from what I saw in the film --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before -- wait a minute. Before you come to what you think, let's just move a few pages further on, and that's on page 261 of the English. And it's when you have Mr. Bucin again. If you continue a little bit in the text, you have Mr. Bucin again, and he is proposing the following: "He then proposed that our solution be that we not impose but, rather, that we announce the possibility of imposing emergency measures and that we not raise combat readiness, but rather announce that I was surprised -- announced that." Mr. Jovic then says, remarks: "I was surprised by his explanation that he has no mandate from his republics for any other decision. He said literally the following: We must announce the possibility of imposing emergency measures and also announce the need to order the highest raised level of combat readiness. I would not want to cross that line this evening in concrete terms. I do not have a mandate from my republic in that sense."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So as we can see here, Mr. Bucin did not agree to the declaration of a state of emergency because his republic had not allowed him to do so. Do you remember that? You were in Montenegro. Do you remember that, that the republic did not want to accept that proposal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was on the delegation of Montenegro to the federal parliament. That's the post I occupied. I must say -- insist on this session very much, and you insist on the positions taken by various individuals at that session, and I didn't attend it. But you seem to interpret it in one way while I interpret it in quite another. Maybe I am wrong in my interpretation, but from what that film of the session that I viewed several times, I believe that Mr. Bucin had throughout occupied a very constructive position, and what you are reading is maybe his attempt during the deliberations to find a constructive solution and take the Presidency out of an impasse. And I have to say that Bucin was in favour, himself, of accepting the proposal of the General Staff, but because the Presidency seemed to be in a tie and it seemed unable to take the decisions that would make it possible to save Yugoslavia and prevent civil war, Mr. Bucin resigned. I am sorry for taking your time, but I think it was important to be said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the Montenegrin leadership explicitly ordered Bucin not to accept the proposal. Do you know that? I mean, you are from Montenegro, and you were a part of it at that time. You know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But earlier in my evidence, I have also said that the mandate of a member to the Presidency of the SFRY from any republic is not imperative in nature. In other words, nobody from the leadership of Montenegro could have -- may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kostic, I simply asked you, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let him finish what he was saying, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Mr. Bucin is concerned, nobody from the leadership of Montenegro could have given him orders, had the right to give him orders not to accept this proposal of the Supreme Command. Only the Assembly of Montenegro that appointed him to the SFRY Presidency could have given him that instruction. And as far as I know, the Assembly of Montenegro, which is the only one who had those powers, did not give such instructions to Mr. Bucin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to continue further in this book of Mr. Jovic. Mr. Jovic actually speaks under his note for the 13th of March, 1991. He refers -- he says the following -- he refers to a meeting with General Kadijevic and Slobodan Milosevic, and it's during this session, ongoing session: "Veljko literally told us in the presence of General Adzic, we are going to stage a military coup regardless of whether or not the proposed decision is adopted. If it is adopted, then it will give us cover for mobilisation only during the first 48 hours, but if it is rejected, we will conduct mobilisation on our own. In that case, however, there is the danger that the Presidency will meet and depose the military leadership. That is why we need a decision." Then after a question of Mr. Jovic what he means by a military coup, he responded: "Deposing the government and the Presidency. They will not touch the Assembly, but neither will they allow it to convene. They will not touch the republican authorities and all the others if they support the coup, otherwise they will be removed as well." Mr. Kostic, that's actually what he refers to as a military coup and a removal of the republican leaderships that do not support that. That means Serbia and perhaps Montenegro if they change their minds. They remain in power, the others not. That was discussed at that time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think your conclusion is correct. If a military coup had happened, then it would have implied the toppling and detention or isolation of all members of the Presidency of the SFRY from all republics, including Serbia and Montenegro. No distinctions would have been made. But I cannot be asked to interpret here the opinion of Mr. Jovic or any other member of the Presidency. I can only say that if a military coup had been staged, then it would have affected all bodies of authority in all republics. And I've even said earlier in my testimony - but that's my political assessment - it's possible that a military coup would have been more efficient and quicker in resolving the Yugoslav crisis, like what we saw in Greece, the military junta eventually replaced military rule with democracy eight years later, when problems were resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, could you give the page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The page -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic's comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- just one other question: Is the suggestion that Mr. Bucin abstained in the vote?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. He did not declare this. And actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- what I wanted to put to you, you said it was a four-to-four deadlock, but looking at Mr. Jovic's book, it's actually, and he says it, indeed, he says it on page -- what is the page? In his reference to the 14th of March, 1991, Mr. Jovic actually says it was not a four-to-four, surprisingly for him, but he says, "Riza Sapundzija changed his mind and it was three against five." This is what Mr. Jovic says, and it's book page 264. And Mr. Kostic, given that Mr. Jovic was the president and actually present during this meeting, says there was no deadlock situation at that point in time, there was actually a firm majority against declaration of emergency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're putting that to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's -- that's how it was, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I left that as an open possibility in what I said earlier, because I said I didn't know what Riza Sapundzija decided and how he voted in every round. I said it was a possibility, and I suppose that Mr. Jovic is correct in what he says, because he was there. He was the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would mean, though, that Bucin also voted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He did not -- yeah. He did not support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you read the next sentence. "When we complete the voting and concluded that the decision had not been adopted."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I've put my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on, but it's time to adjourn already.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At least this is my understanding, that Mr. Bucin was not allowed to vote because he had -- he had this -- this recommendations from his Montenegro president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not in the middle of negotiation? But we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will have to adjourn. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
